```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

energyRt's test suite is large -- 162 files, 1,280 `test_that` blocks, 28,000
lines -- but its size is not the interesting part. What makes it work is a small
number of deliberate choices, each made because something went wrong first. This
article is the **why**: what the suite is organised around, what guarantee each
mechanism actually gives you, and what it deliberately does not test. For the
*how* -- the recipes for adding a test -- see the reference in `tests/README.md`.

It is written for contributors. If you only want to run the suite, the one thing
to know is that it is **tiered**, and the tier decides whether a solver runs at
all:

```{r}
Sys.setenv(ENERGYRT_TEST_TIER = "fast")   # the default outside R CMD check
devtools::test()
```

# The organising principle is the model, not the code

Line coverage answers "was this line executed". For a modelling package that is
the wrong question. The one that matters is **"is this model parameter ever
actually constrained by a test?"** -- and a line-coverage tool cannot tell you,
because a parameter can be written, interpolated, handed to a solver, and never
bind anything.

So coverage is tracked over the **model vocabulary**: every set, mapping,
numeric parameter, bound, equation and variable the package can emit. There are
747 of them, enumerated in `tests/coverage/parameter-matrix.csv`.

Tests declare what they cover with a tag:

```{r}
# @covers pTechRampUp pTechRampDown depth=S backends=glpk forks=fx,fold
test_that("ramp limits constrain dispatch", { ... })
```

The names must be **model vocabulary, never R function names**. There is no
matrix row for `read_solution()`, so a tag naming it is a typo that fails the
suite (`tools/coverage/build_matrix.R --check`). Coverage of the R API is
recorded as a plain comment instead -- `# Covers the R API: levcost()` -- which
is documentation rather than a tracked claim.

`depth=` records how far a test actually goes, and it is the honest part of the
scheme:

| depth | meaning |
|---|---|
| `C` | the parameter is **c**onstructed -- it appears in the built input |
| `I` | it survives **i**nterpolation into `modInp` |
| `S` | a **s**olve runs and the parameter is in the model |
| `X` | the solved result is checked against an e**x**pected number |

Only `X` is a behavioural guarantee. A row at `C` means almost nothing, and the
matrix says so rather than reporting a flattering percentage.

One sharp edge: those meanings describe a **hand-written tag**, where the author
asserts the depth. Where no tag exists, `build_matrix.R` *infers* a depth from
the file's text, and its proxy for `X` is cruder -- "the file solves and mentions
at least two backends" (`file_depth()`). So an `inferred` `X` does not mean any
test checked a number; it means the file looked like a cross-backend solve test.
Read `covered_depth` together with `status`, never alone.

Current adoption: **139 tags across 53 of 162 files**. The remaining 109 fall
back to keyword inference, marked `inferred` in the matrix, which should not be
read as a tagged claim.

# Tiers, not `skip_on_cran()`

Solver-dependent tests were once gated with `skip_on_cran()`. That failed in the
worst way available: on a machine without a solver the tests **silently passed**.
A green suite meant nothing, and nobody could tell.

Tiers replace it (`tests/testthat/helper-solvers.R`):

| tier | value | what runs |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | 0 | no solver, no network -- what `R CMD check` gets |
| `fast` | 1 | GLPK only; the default in a dev session |
| `cross` | 2 | Julia, Pyomo, GAMS, NEOS -- backend parity |
| `nightly` | 3 | the full suite, including the slowest models |

Two details carry the design:

* `en_test_tier()` **errors** on an unrecognised value rather than falling back
  to a default. A typo in `ENERGYRT_TEST_TIER` stops the run instead of quietly
  testing less than you asked for.
* Unset, it resolves to `check` under `R CMD check` and `fast` otherwise, so the
  strict environment is the automatic one.

The honest caveat: only **6** call sites use `skip_if_tier_below()` directly. In
practice the tier is carried by the skip guards, and `skip_if_no_solver()` --
437 uses -- is the real gate. It opens with `skip_if_tier_below("fast")` and
then probes for `glpsol`; every cross-backend guard opens with
`skip_if_tier_below("cross")`. So the tier is a property of the *guards*, and
adding a guard is how a test joins a tier.

# Goldens are gated on invariants, not on being green

A reference objective is meaningful only if the solution it came from was itself
coherent. So `tools/test/make_goldens.R` **refuses to freeze** a benchmark that
fails `verify_solution()`:

```
REFUSED: 'tm_core' fails solution invariants -- fix the model or the code
before freezing a benchmark.
```

That refusal is the point of the mechanism. Without it, a golden records
whatever the solver happened to emit -- including a quietly wrong answer -- and
every later run compares against it faithfully.

Tolerances are per comparison kind, not one global number:

| comparison | tolerance | why |
|---|---|---|
| same solver, re-run | `1e-9` | only floating-point noise is legitimate |
| cross-solver objective | `1e-6` | different algorithms, same optimum |
| cross-solver aggregates | `1e-5` | degenerate optima redistribute within a total |

**Per-timeslice values are deliberately not stored.** Where an LP has multiple
optima the per-slice split is solver-specific while the aggregate is not.
Storing the split would give you a test that fails on a solver upgrade and tells
you nothing.

## The second golden: interpolation itself

An objective can be unchanged while the model that produced it has changed
underneath. `tools/test/interp_guard.R` therefore freezes `modInp` -- the
interpolated input -- and diffs it structurally with `compare_inputs()`:

```
Parameters: 502 common | identical: 502 | differing: 0
  only in base: pTradeIrCost
  only in cur:  pTradeIrVarom
```

That is real output from a parameter rename, and it is exactly what the guard is
for: a change no objective comparison could see. Re-freeze only for an intended
change, in the same commit, with a NEWS entry.

# Fork families: one model, several ways

Many of this package's defects have not been "this number is wrong" but "this
number is right on one path and wrong on another". So the families
(`test-family-*.R`, 18 files) push one small model through several forks --
`fx`, `fold`, `ondisk`, `sparse`, `prune`, `vintage`, `cluster`, `sampled`,
`geoframe` -- and assert they agree.

Backend parity is the same idea across writers: GLPK, Julia/JuMP, Python/Pyomo
and GAMS must produce the same objective from the same model. It is the only
mechanism that catches a bug living in a single template.

# What the suite does not test

Worth knowing before you trust a green run.

**`verify_solution()` has a structural blind spot.** It replays the model's
identities from the *same mappings* the writers used. If a mapping is missing a
domain, the check and the model are wrong in the same direction and agree. In
August 2026 a coarse-geoscale supply bug produced a model that solved to
objective **0** with every invariant reporting "ok". Invariants catch
inconsistency, not absence.

**There is no CI.** `.github/` holds no workflows. The tier mechanism is built so
CI needs no test changes, and `tests/README.md` specifies a three-job design,
but nothing runs on push. Every number in this article comes from someone running
the suite by hand.

**There is no expected-failure baseline.** Nothing records which failures are
known, so a new failure cannot be told from an old one without investigating it.
That has a measurable cost: of three failures recently carried in the suite, two
were stale hand-written counts and one was a genuine package defect -- and
separating them took measurement, not a lookup.

**Snapshots and hand-written counts go stale silently.** Both assert facts about
regenerated metadata. When a legitimate new mapping landed, the coverage CSV was
refreshed and committed, but a hard-coded `308` in `test-coverage-matrix.R` and
an accepted snapshot were not -- so a generated artefact and its own guard
disagreed for two weeks. Prefer a regenerated, tracked file to an integer typed
into a test.

**A nightly-only guard is only as good as the nightly.** `interp_guard` correctly
reported drift for 15 days across five commits and nobody saw it, because the
test that runs it is nightly-tier and no nightly had run. A guard nobody executes
is documentation.

# Conventions

* **Tiers, not `skip_on_cran()`.** If a test needs a solver, guard it.
* **Tag model vocabulary, not functions.** Use `# Covers the R API: f()` for the
  rest.
* **Pin a defect you cannot fix yet.** Assert the *broken* behaviour with
  `KNOWN BUG:` in the test name, a dated note, and a label saying what to flip
  when it is fixed, so the eventual fix fails loudly instead of passing quietly.
* **A guard must be able to fail.** Write it, then break something deliberately
  and watch it go red. A regex typo once left a new guard incapable of failing;
  only the negative test found it.
* **An aborted run is not a passing run.** Check the exit code, not the absence
  of red.
